keyTerms.definition: The instructors of Machine Learning (Stanford CS229), listed for the Lesson 04 keys dated 2026-10-06.
The format of the U04 lesson answer keys, intended to be kept separate from other work.
The course containing Lesson 04, which covers generative classifiers and their corresponding answer keys.
The answer key section for Unit 04 on generative classifiers within the Machine Learning (Stanford CS229) course.

recall.question: Who are the instructors listed for Lesson 04 keys?
recall.answer: The instructors are Tengyu Ma and Andrew Ng.

recall.question: What is the date and answer format for the Lesson 04 keys?
recall.answer: The date is 2026-10-06. The answers are closed-book and should be kept separate.

keyTerms.definition: The probability density function of a multivariate Gaussian, defined as 1/((2 pi)^{d/2} |Sigma|^{1/2}) times the exponential of negative half the Mahalanobis distance.
The covariance matrix appearing in the Gaussian density, whose inverse and determinant scale and shape the distribution.

recall.question: Write the full formula for the multivariate Gaussian density p(x, mu, Sigma) as shown in the section.
recall.answer: p(x, mu, Sigma) = 1/((2 pi)^{d/2} |Sigma|^{1/2}) exp(-(1/2)(x - mu)^T Sigma^{-1} (x - mu)). It pairs a normalization constant with the exponential of negative half the quadratic form.

keyTerms.definition: The mean of y in the model formulation, serving as a baseline parameter alongside the class means and covariance.
The covariance matrix computed as the average over all training samples of the outer product of each sample minus its class mean.

recall.question: How is the common covariance matrix Sigma defined in this section?
recall.answer: Sigma equals (1/n) times the sum over all training samples of (x^{(i)} minus mu_{y^{(i)}}) times its transpose. This estimate pools information across all classes by using each sample's own class mean.

keyTerms.definition: The natural logarithm of the ratio of probabilities for a class, here expressed as log p(x|y=1) minus log p(x|y=0) plus log odds(phi).
Refers to using the same covariance matrix for all classes, which causes the quadratic x terms to cancel out.

recall.question: Why do the quadratic terms cancel in the log odds expression when Sigma is shared?
recall.answer: With shared Sigma, the -(1/2) x^T Sigma^{-1} x terms cancel out, leaving only terms that are linear in x.

keyTerms.definition: It states that the joint probability factors into the product of individual feature probabilities given the class label.
It is the joint probability of all feature values given a class label y.

recall.question: What does the naive Bayes assumption say about the joint probability p(x_1, ..., x_d | y)?
recall.answer: It factors into the product of the individual conditional probabilities p(x_j | y) over all features j.

keyTerms.definition: A probability value for class j given label y, computed with add-one Laplace smoothing.
A smoothing technique applied by adding one to the numerator count and two to the denominator count.

recall.question: What formula gives phi_{j|y} for class j given label y?
recall.answer: phi_{j|y} equals one plus count_{j,y} divided by two plus n_y. This applies add-one Laplace smoothing to the count.

keyTerms.definition: A model where the email is a per-word presence checklist.
A model where the email is a sequence of word draws.

recall.question: How does the Bernoulli event model represent an email?
recall.answer: The Bernoulli event model represents the email as a per-word presence checklist.

keyTerms.definition: A parameter set to 0.5 in this section, likely representing a prior probability or mixing proportion.
The mean for class 0, set to 1 in this example.
The mean for class 1, set to 6 in this example.
The pooled covariance value computed as 1, derived from averaging class variances.

recall.question: What is the value of phi in this section?
recall.answer: The value of phi is set to 0.5 in this section.

recall.question: What are the centered values for class 0 and class 1?
recall.answer: Class 0 has centered values of -1 and 1, and class 1 also has centered values of -1 and 1.

keyTerms.definition: A function whose value is linear in x after quadratic terms cancel, used here to separate the two classes.
The inverse of the shared covariance matrix S, which scales the linear and constant terms in the decision function.

recall.question: Why is the decision function linear in x after the quadratic terms are removed?
recall.answer: The x^T S^{-1} x terms cancel out. What remains is x^T S^{-1}(mu1 - mu0) plus a constant, which is linear in x.

keyTerms.definition: A problem where predicted probabilities do not match true likelihoods, even when overall accuracy is acceptable.
Evidence that is counted more than once by a model, causing naive Bayes to produce overconfident probability estimates.
A post-hoc calibration method that fits a logistic regression to map model scores into calibrated probabilities.
A post-hoc calibration method that learns a nondecreasing mapping from scores to probabilities using validation data.

recall.question: What is the diagnosis for section E09?
recall.answer: The model shows miscalibration from double-counted evidence, typical of naive Bayes overconfidence. Accuracy is fine, but the probabilities are not.

recall.question: How can the miscalibration described in E09 be fixed?
recall.answer: Apply post-hoc calibration such as Platt scaling or isotonic regression on validation data, or switch to a discriminative model.

keyTerms.definition: The logistic regression approach that wins at n = 1e6 because Poisson features make the Gaussian assumption wrong.
An assumption that is wrong when features follow a Poisson distribution in the large-data limit.
The GDA approach that may win at n = 100 since GDA has fewer effective parameters to estimate.
The recommended method to check both approaches honestly and decide which performs better.

recall.question: Which team wins at n = 1e6 and why?
recall.answer: Team B (logistic) wins at n = 1e6 because with Poisson features the Gaussian assumption is wrong, and in the large-data limit the weaker assumptions win.

recall.question: Which team may win at n = 100 and on what basis?
recall.answer: Team A may win at n = 100 on the basis of variance, since GDA has fewer effective parameters to estimate. The honest answer is to check both with validation.

keyTerms.definition: The distance s between the means of two Gaussian distributions in the E11 setup.
Gaussian Discriminant Analysis, a classifier fit on the two Gaussians for each sample size n.
Logistic regression, a classifier fit on the same data for each sample size n.
The sample size at which logistic regression's test error drops below GDA's test error.

recall.question: What values of mean separation s and sample size n does the E11 experiment use?
recall.answer: Mean separation s takes values in {0.5, 1, 2, 4}, and sample size n takes values in {50, 100, 500, 2000, 10000}.

recall.question: What claim does E11 make about the crossover n between logistic and GDA?
recall.answer: E11 claims the crossover n where logistic beats GDA grows as the mean separation s shrinks. It is falsified if logistic never wins or wins at the same n for all s.

keyTerms.definition: A list of unique words used as the vocabulary index for mapping words to position numbers in the code.
A dictionary mapping each class label to a NumPy array that tracks how many times each vocabulary word appears for that class.
A dictionary mapping each class to its probability distribution over the vocabulary, computed by dividing counts by their sum.
A list of integer class labels, where 1 or 0 indicates the class for each corresponding document.

recall.question: How does the code compute the probability distribution for each class?
recall.answer: It divides each class counts array by its sum, producing a probability distribution for that class over the vocabulary.

recall.question: What does the assertion at the end of the code check?
recall.answer: It checks that each class probability distribution sums to 1.0 within a tolerance of 1e-12.

keyTerms.definition: A generative classifier that models x|y as Gaussian with class-specific means and a shared covariance Sigma.
The sum of log p(x_i, y_i) used to fit GDA parameters by separating per-class terms.
Adding a ridge regularizer to the shared covariance to fix singularities from too few points or collinearity.
Quadratic Discriminant Analysis, used when real classes do not share covariance.

recall.question: Why does GDA beat logistic regression for small n on Gaussian data, and when does logistic catch up?
recall.answer: With Gaussian data and small n, GDA wins because it uses the correct generative model. As n grows, logistic regression catches up in performance.

recall.question: What can cause Sigma to become singular in GDA, and how is it fixed?
recall.answer: Sigma becomes singular when there are fewer independent points than dimensions, or when features are collinear. Fix it by adding a ridge term to Sigma or by dropping features.

keyTerms.definition: A classifier that assumes feature independence, decomposing p(x|y) into a product of per-feature conditional probabilities across tokens.
A fix for unseen features that would otherwise zero out the product, applied to keep all probability entries strictly positive.
A naive Bayes variant suited to short documents that avoids being overwhelmed by absence terms.
A naive Bayes variant that wins on long documents, here implemented with Laplace smoothing and a tuned threshold.

recall.question: Why does the product p(x|y) collapse to zero when a feature is unseen, and how is it fixed?
recall.answer: An unseen feature multiplies by zero, which zeroes the whole product. The fix is Laplace smoothing, which keeps every entry positive.

recall.question: When does multinomial naive Bayes beat the Bernoulli variant, and why?
recall.answer: Multinomial wins on long documents. On short documents Bernoulli is competitive because the multinomial gets drowned in absence terms.
